title: The overdraft rule
dek: A federal rule to limit what the largest banks charge for overdrafts, and the resolution that undid it before it took effect.
regulators: Comptroller of the Currency|\bOCC\b|FDIC|Federal Deposit Insurance|Federal Reserve|\bCFPB\b|Consumer Financial Protection|Department of the Treasury|Treasury Department|\bSEC\b|Securities and Exchange|NCUA|National Credit Union|FHFA|Federal Housing Finance|Banking Committee|Committee on Banking|Financial Services Committee|Committee on Financial Services

facts.text: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau finalizes a rule on overdraft fees at banks and credit unions with more than $10 billion in assets. Each could charge $5, charge no more than its costs and losses, or treat overdrafts as loans under the lending laws, with the interest rate disclosed.

source.title: CFPB press release, Dec. 12, 2024 (reprinted by CUInsight)

facts.text: The bureau estimates the rule would save consumers up to $5 billion a year in overdraft fees, about $225 for each household that pays them.

source.title: CFPB press release, Dec. 12, 2024 (reprinted by CUInsight)

facts.text: The rule is published: "Overdraft Lending: Very Large Financial Institutions," 89 Fed. Reg. 106768, to take effect October 1, 2025.
The Senate passes S.J.Res. 18, a Congressional Review Act resolution disapproving the rule, 52 to 48.
The President signs it: Public Law 119-10. The rule has no force or effect, and under the Congressional Review Act the bureau may not issue a substantially similar rule unless Congress authorizes it.

not_yet: Lobbying reports that describe the rule in words, without naming either resolution, are not counted yet: 36 organizations mentioned overdraft in report text from January 2025 to March 2026.
